title: Harmlessness
hook: the intention not to harm, even in thought

segments.voice: Yesterday: goodwill, and your line, steer by goodwill. Did one conversation get steered kindly, even a little, when it pushed back? Day three hundred sixty-four, the end of the week.

Credit for an idea gets taken in a meeting, and on the drive home a little film starts to play. In the film, the person who took it trips on the stairs. Their coffee spills down their shirt. Their car gets a flat in the rain. Nobody is badly hurt, of course. Just enough. Nobody acts on it. A film like that can run for a long time before anyone notices it's running. The Buddha noticed. Before his awakening, he says, he caught thoughts of harming in his own mind and put them in the bad pile, right beside ill will. Today, the last of the three right intentions: harmlessness, all the way down into thought.
screen: `CREDIT TAKEN IN A MEETING.` → `A LITTLE FILM STARTS.` → `JUST ENOUGH HARM.`

segments.voice: The word on our list is ahimsa, a word Pali and Sanskrit share: the not-harming that Jains and Hindus hold dear as well. In the Pali list of right intentions, the word is avihiṃsā, non-cruelty: the intention not to harm. Yesterday's goodwill was about not wishing ill. This one leans closer to action: not wanting anyone to suffer, and not wanting to be the cause. In the sutta of the two kinds of thought, the Buddha is plain about thoughts of harming. When one arose in him, he saw that it led to his own affliction, to the affliction of others, or to both, and that it led away from wisdom. As he considered that, he says, it subsided. So harm starts upstream, in the film, long before a hand moves. The Dhammapada gives the reason in one line, in Max Müller's words: "All men tremble at punishment, all men fear death; remember that you are like unto them, and do not kill, nor cause slaughter." You are like them. That's the whole argument. A later verse says a person isn't called noble for injuring living creatures, but for having pity on all of them. Later teachers pair harmlessness with compassion, karuṇā: it's the soil compassion grows in. Look back at the week. The blind men, each holding a part. Intend it. Two piles. Guard, then rest. The relief of less. Steer by goodwill. And today, no harm meant. Three right intentions, one direction.
screen: `AVIHIṂSĀ: THE INTENTION NOT TO HARM.` · `HARM STARTS UPSTREAM.` · `YOU ARE LIKE THEM.` · `THE SOIL COMPASSION GROWS IN.` · then, large: `NO HARM MEANT.`

segments.voice: Sit comfortably and let the breath find its own pace. Now, gently, look for the film. Is there anyone you've been quietly wishing a small misfortune on? A coworker, a neighbor, someone on the news? Don't scold yourself for finding it. Just catch it, the way you'd catch a glass before it hits the floor. Then do what the Dhammapada suggests: remember they're like you. They flinch at pain too. Let the film stop there. The bell holds the time.
Ahimsa. Not harming. In the Buddha's list it's avihiṃsā, the intention not to harm, the third right intention.
Your line: no harm meant. Today, catch one harmful thought before the film finishes, and let it end unfinished. Day three hundred sixty-four, and a week done.

howItsDone: Lay Buddhists take the first precept, not to kill, as the outward form of harmlessness; some also reflect on verses like Dhammapada 129 or practice compassion meditation toward beings who suffer.

fork.setup: someone has wronged you, and the little film is running. what reason does Dhammapada 129 give for not harming them?
options: they tremble at punishment and fear death, just as you do.
fork.reveal: the verse rests on likeness, not on fear or rules: all fear death, so remember that you are like unto them.

original.note: Sanskrit and Pali ahiṃsā: not harming; the Pali right-intention list uses its close cousin avihiṃsā, non-cruelty.

trapdoor: what you thought: ahimsa just means not being violent.
what it means: the intention not to harm, starting in thought, the third right intention.
what a scholar hears: the path definition uses avihiṃsā, non-cruelty, a negative form, and later teachers pair it with karuṇā, as non-ill-will is paired with mettā.

notes: Check Müller's exact wording of Dhammapada 129 in SBE 10.
Index word is 'ahimsa' (Sanskrit); the Pali right-intention term is avihiṃsā. Script explains both. The Keeper may prefer the index word changed to avihimsa.
MN 19 paraphrased: a thought of harming leads to one's own affliction, others' affliction, both, obstructs wisdom, and subsides when so seen.
Pairing of avihiṃsā with karuṇā and abyāpāda with mettā is a commentarial/teacher convention; phrased as 'later teachers'.
